channel.description: ENN | Egui News Network reports from Japan on the side of Japanese history and culture that schools never teach: the plots, the scandals, the executions and the quiet deals behind the beautiful image of Japan. If you love Japan, this is the Japan behind the postcard, told straight in plain English. Read the full stories on Substack, and get the collected editions as books on Amazon.

item.title: The Sengoku Period Explained: How Succession Fights Created Japan's Warlords
item.description:
A young man killed his half-brother and his half-brother's mother, and seized by force the seat that ruled eastern Japan. The man sent to strike him down was Hojo Soun. The Warring States period was an age born from fights over who would inherit each house. In the shogun's family and in the warlords' families alike, every succession fight produced a new master. And when three houses that had won their succession fights joined hands, a man standing outside their circle, Oda Nobunaga, ended up bringing the age to a close.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/sengoku-period/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Muromachi Period Explained: Two Ashikaga Houses and the Brakes That Failed
item.description:
At a victory banquet, warriors burst in and cut down the guest of honor: the shogun himself. And this shogun, Ashikaga Yoshinori, had been chosen by drawing lots. The Muromachi shogunate was a system with two Ashikaga houses standing side by side: the shogun in Kyoto, and the Kamakura kubo in Kamakura. What kept them from colliding was the people in the middle who acted as brakes. Every time a brake was lost, war broke out, and in the end, Kyoto itself was burned to the ground in the Onin War.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/muromachi-period/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Nanbokucho Period Explained: Why the Weaker Southern Court Lasted Sixty Years
item.description:
For about sixty years, Japan had two emperors at once. The Southern Court of Emperor Go-Daigo, holed up in the mountains of Yoshino, lost almost all of the commanders it relied on within a few years. So why did it last until 1392? The answer: it was not Southern strength. The Northern side split apart in family quarrels again and again, and every time, the side that was about to lose borrowed the Southern Court's banner. This episode follows the sixty years of the two courts along that answer.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/nanbokucho-period/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Kenmu Restoration: How Go-Daigo and Takauji Fell Out Over Three Seals of Approval
item.description:
Emperor Go-Daigo finally ruled Japan himself. About three years later, the warrior who had won him that power drove him out of Kyoto. The answer: the two men were fighting over three seals of approval. This episode follows their struggle over who leads the warriors, who hands out land to retainers, and whose war is a just one.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/kenmu-restoration/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Fall of the Kamakura Shogunate: Why Emperor Go-Daigo Won on His Third Try
item.description:
A warrior government that lasted about a hundred and fifty years collapsed in just a few weeks. Why did Emperor Go-Daigo fail twice, and win on his third try? The answer: the shogunate fell when its own warriors gave up on it. This episode follows Go-Daigo's three attempts in order, and shows what changed.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/fall-of-the-kamakura-shogunate/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Kamakura Shogunate Explained: The Promise of Land That Built It and Broke It
item.description:
What held Japan's first warrior government together for about a hundred and fifty years? One promise: risk your life in battle, and you will be rewarded with land. As long as the shogunate could keep it, it was strong. When it could not, everything began to fall apart. This episode follows the Kamakura period through four scenes: the promise is born, it changes hands, it is put to the test, and it breaks.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/kamakura-period/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Genpei War Explained: Four Challengers Who Brought Down the Taira
item.description:
Who really brought down the Taira, the family at the top of Japan? Not a single hero, but four challengers, each holding a different trump card: a prince with a written order, a general who seized the capital, a genius of the battlefield, and a man who never once stood on the front line. This episode walks you through the Genpei War, the six years from 1180 to 1185 that ended at Dan-no-ura.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/genpei-war/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Heian Period Explained: The Grandfathers Who Really Ran Japan
item.description:
Who really ran Japan during the four hundred years of the Heian period? Not the emperor, but the emperor's grandfather: first the Fujiwara regents, then the retired emperors, and finally Taira no Kiyomori. This episode walks you through the Heian period, from the founding of Heian-kyo in 794 to the fall of the Taira at Dan-no-ura in 1185.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/heian-period/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Nara Period Explained: Why Japan's Capital Lasted Only 84 Years
item.description:
Why did Japan's grand capital at Nara last only 84 years? The answer is three shocks that hit the country again and again: feuds between powerful families, epidemics and disasters, and the fight over who would inherit the throne. This episode walks you through the Nara period, from the founding of Heijo-kyo to the move to Heian-kyo.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/nara-period/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Asuka Period in 4 Minutes: How Japan Became an Emperor's Nation
item.description:
How did Japan go from a loose group of powerful clans to a nation ruled by the emperor? The answer is three events: a religious war, a palace coup, and a civil war within the royal family. This episode walks you through the Asuka period, from the arrival of Buddhism to the founding of Nara.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/asuka-period/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: Japanese History for Beginners: The Whole Story in 18 Minutes
item.description:
How did Japan go from Ice Age hunters to one of the world's largest economies? The answer fits in one line: the imperial court, the shogunate, the modern nation, war, and recovery. This first episode walks you through every era of Japanese history, with no dates to memorize, just the big picture.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/japanese-history/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com
